candidateRows: A genuine secular basis for morality is possible, so God is not necessary for objective distinctions between right and wrong.
This explicitly identifies the central question as whether morality can have a non-theistic basis and states the con side's answer.
After distinguishing moral motivation from moral grounding, Kagan narrows the debate to whether genuine right and wrong can exist on a secular basis.
Right and wrong can be grounded in whether conduct harms people or unjustifiably fails to help them.
The harm-and-help account supplies the substantive moral standard that anchors Kagan's proposed non-theistic explanation of ordinary duties.
Kagan presents harm and failures to help as the basis of right and wrong, then connects that principle to familiar prohibitions and duties.
Objective moral facts consist in overriding categorical reasons that do not depend on anyone's opinions, desires, or goals.
This directly defends secular moral objectivity by explaining both the truth of moral claims and their desire-independent normative force.
The anticipated objection that atheistic morality is merely subjective opinion rather than a genuine fact.
Kagan argues that rape remains wrong regardless of individual or collective approval because everyone has strong, overriding reasons not to inflict such harm.
Secular moral realism may treat categorical moral reasons as basic objective facts requiring no deeper foundation.
The move answers the demand for an ultimate foundation by denying that every objective moral truth must be derived from something deeper.
The anticipated demand that secular categorical reasons must have some further ultimate basis or source.
Kagan notes disagreement among secular philosophers and explains that non-foundationalists regard categorical reasons and moral rules as irreducible facts of reality.
Contractarian morality is objective because its rules are those perfectly rational agents would agree to behind a veil of ignorance.
This provides a positive deeper secular grounding for moral rules and explains why their content can be both objective and necessary.
Kagan sketches rational agreement under fair informational constraints, then locates moral objectivity in facts about what perfectly rational agents necessarily would choose.
Moral requirements need no personal lawgiver, just as the requirement of non-contradiction needs no cosmic logician.
The analogy directly challenges a principal inference from objective moral obligation to God and preserves genuine duties within secular realism.
The theistic contention that every genuine commandment, moral law, or requirement logically presupposes a personal commander or lawgiver.
Kagan compares morality with rational non-contradiction, arguing that objective requirements can arise from decisive reasons without being issued by a person.
Even if moral requirements need issuers, rational members of the moral community can impose those requirements on one another.
This supplies an alternative secular answer to the lawgiver argument even after provisionally granting its disputed requirement-to-issuer premise.
The claim that if moral requirements must be issued by someone, only God could possess the authority to issue them.
Using his contractarian framework, Kagan argues that rational agents mutually authorize rules and may legitimately demand compliance from themselves and others.
Without God, objective moral values, objective moral duties, and ultimate moral accountability would not exist.
This is Craig's explicit roadmap and overarching proposition, organizing his entire affirmative case around three distinct dependencies on God.
Kagan's preceding thesis that secular moral realism can sustain genuine objective morality without appealing to God.
Craig distinguishes actual morality from mere behavioral convention and announces that values, duties, and accountability each require God.
God's nature grounds objective moral value, whereas atheistic naturalism reduces human worth and morality to contingent evolutionary adaptations.
The move supplies Craig's principal argument that objective value requires a transcendent standard and cannot survive a naturalistic account of humanity.
Kagan's claim that categorical reasons and rational agreement can establish objective moral facts on a secular basis.
Craig defines objectivity, locates its standard in God's loving nature, and argues that naturalism yields evolved herd morality rather than genuine human worth.
Objective moral duties require a divine lawgiver because atheistic social conditioning or social contracts cannot create genuine obligations.
This directly contests the secular grounding of obligation and constitutes one of the three independently announced pillars of Craig's affirmative case.
Kagan's argument that moral requirements can rest on categorical reason or the mutual authority of rational contractors without God.
Craig distinguishes duties from values, grounds obligations in commands flowing from God's nature, and argues that atheism leaves only conventions comparable to etiquette.
Moral responsibility applies to rational agents because they can reflect on reasons and regulate their behavior, unlike animals or very young children.
The response supplies a secular explanation for why harming others can be objectively wrong for humans even when comparable animal behavior is not morally culpable.
Craig's challenge that naturalism cannot explain why human harm is wrong when animals routinely harm one another.
Craig asks why harm among humans is morally different from harm among animals; Kagan grounds the distinction in an agent's capacity to recognize and respond to reasons.
Once rational agents can recognize reasons against harmful conduct, no additional supernatural ingredient is required for objective wrongness.
This directly advances the secular realist thesis that objective moral reasons and wrongness can arise from rational agency without a divine lawgiver.
Craig's objection that rational reflection may be necessary for morality but is not sufficient to make harmful conduct wrong.
After Craig demands a sufficient condition for morality, Kagan argues that reasons recognizable by sufficiently rational creatures provide the essential basis of wrongness.
Naturalism has not adequately grounded the intrinsic value of persons merely by identifying the remarkable capacities that humans possess.
The challenge targets the debate's foundational issue: whether secular descriptions of human capacities can explain objective value rather than merely presuppose it.
Kagan's claim that human capacities for reflection, love, creativity, and communication make persons distinctively valuable.
Craig accepts that people intuitively value persons and their capacities but argues that naturalism still owes a deeper account of why those features are objectively good.
The absence of eternal cosmic meaning does not entail that ethics is illusory or that human life lacks meaningful moral significance.
This separates finite moral significance from cosmic permanence and directly contests the theistic claim that secular mortality empties ethics of genuine meaning.
Craig's opening reliance on the claim that without theism ethics and deeper human meaning become illusory.
Kagan grants that naturalism lacks meaning on an eternal cosmic scale but asks why that concession should undermine ethics or the significance available within human life.
Because naturalism ends in universal extinction without ultimate accountability, human moral choices lack enduring significance and leave the universe no better or worse.
The passage states the pro side's central case that objective accountability and ultimate significance require a theistic framework extending beyond temporal human consequences.
Kagan's objection that rejecting eternal cosmic meaning gives no reason to regard ethics or finite human significance as illusory.
Craig invokes the eventual heat death of the universe and the absence of postmortem accountability to argue that every moral outcome ultimately collapses into the same result.
Torture matters objectively to victims, families, and communities even if it never changes the universe's eternal endpoint.
The argument supplies a direct secular account of genuine moral significance and denies that objective importance must be eternal or cosmically scaled.
Craig's claim that finite moral choices become insignificant because all life and consequences eventually disappear in cosmic heat death.
Kagan argues that the suffering of torture victims plainly matters to them and others, and that no eternal alteration of the cosmos is needed for this importance to be real.
Even granting objective duties on atheism, prudential self-interest can conflict with morality, whereas divine accountability ultimately brings the two into harmony.
This refines the accountability argument from the existence of duties to the rational motivation for following them when sacrifice conflicts with personal advantage.
Kagan's insistence that objective categorical moral reasons remain binding even without affecting the universe's final cosmic state.
Craig grants moral duties for purposes of the argument but says atheism leaves prudence and morality in collision, while eventual divine justice reconciles sacrifice with ultimate self-interest.
A conflict between morality and prudence does not show that prudential reasons prevail; naturalism can hold that moral reasons carry greater rational weight.
The response blocks Craig's motivational argument by denying that rational action under naturalism must prioritize self-interest over independent moral reasons.
Craig's argument that without divine accountability prudential self-interest would trump morality whenever the two conflict.
Kagan accepts that prudence and morality may diverge but argues that this alone does not determine their relative authority or commit naturalists to privileging prudence.
The social-contract standard condemns Nazi conduct objectively because rational bargainers behind fair constraints would prohibit killing innocent people.
The answer demonstrates how secular contractarianism can condemn atrocities independently of popularity, historical victory, actual consent, or prevailing convention.
The audience challenge that Nazi conduct might cease to be objectively wrong if the Nazis had won and dictated social morality.
Kagan explains that the contract is a rational thought experiment under a veil of ignorance, not a poll, and that its fair terms would forbid the Nazis' actions.
Religious atrocities confirm rather than undermine objective morality, while God remains the transcendent standard needed to move beyond human convention.
The response addresses an apparent counterexample to theism and restates the core grounding claim that objective values require a standard beyond social practices.
The audience objection that numerous historical crimes have been perpetrated in religion's name despite claims of objective theistic morality.
Craig uses the Inquisition, Crusades, and religious intolerance as recognizable evils, then clarifies that his argument concerns God's grounding role rather than belief as a condition of conduct.
Christian salvation through Christ appears to conflict with moral accountability because an evildoer may escape deserved punishment through timely repentance.
The challenge directly tests whether the theistic framework actually secures the moral accountability that Craig presents as an advantage over naturalism.
Craig's claim that theism ensures ultimate punishment, reward, and moral accountability.
Kagan accepts that theism supplies a cosmic enforcer but questions whether Christian forgiveness allows wrongdoers into heaven in tension with accountability.
Christian salvation preserves divine justice because Christ bears the deserved penalty, while repentant sinners receive grace and the self-righteous reject forgiveness.
The response defends the internal coherence of Craig's account of ultimate justice and accountability against a direct objection concerning forgiveness.
Kagan's objection that salvation through Jesus is in tension with genuine moral accountability.
Craig distinguishes repentant sinners from self-righteous people and argues that divine justice is satisfied through Christ's bearing of the penalty for sin.
If grave wrongdoing can be followed by timely acceptance of Jesus and avoidance of punishment, the proposed system does not deliver the asserted accountability.
This rejoinder presses the unresolved consequence of Craig's answer and challenges a principal alleged advantage of theism over secular morality.
Craig's defense that Christ bears the penalty for repentant wrongdoers while preserving divine justice.
Kagan argues that salvation still seems inconsistent with accountability when someone may do evil and later rely on Jesus's saving power.
Theism gives moral life enduring significance because moral choices and deeds genuinely matter, whereas universal extinction casts their importance into doubt.
The claim directly advances the debate's theistic case concerning human significance and the consequences of morality under an atheistic worldview.
Kagan's contention that Christian forgiveness undermines Craig's asserted form of accountability.
Craig redirects the exchange from punishment mechanics to his broader claim that theism makes moral lives consequential and avoids the trivializing effect of cosmic extinction.
Saving a human life remains objectively important even if humanity and the universe eventually perish, so cosmic permanence is unnecessary for significance.
The response directly rejects the proposed inference from eventual cosmic extinction to the absence or diminution of present objective moral significance.
Craig's claim that cosmic extinction renders human deeds and accomplishments trivial or doubtful in significance.
Kagan argues that the importance of saving a person is grounded in the act and its human object, not in whether it has everlasting cosmic consequences.
Because animals such as chickens and cows can be harmed, the secular principles against harming and in favor of helping strongly support vegetarianism and radical reform.
The application demonstrates that Kagan's secular moral realism generates demanding practical duties and challenges Craig's claimed theistic advantage regarding animals.
Craig's claim that naturalism lacks a basis for an ethic governing human treatment of animals.
Kagan applies his harm-and-help account to sentient animals, concluding that common practices involving food, leather, and animal suffering are morally unacceptable.
Cultural moral disagreement concerns fallible access to moral truth rather than its objective existence, and a transcendent standard permits condemnation of corrupt societies.
The argument protects objective morality from the objection based on cultural variation and connects cross-cultural condemnation to Craig's theistic grounding thesis.
Responding to a question about divergent cultures, Craig argues that selfishness and human error explain mistaken codes while objective transcultural morality remains intact.
Secular moral realism can explain historical moral error as gradual discovery enabled by reasoning that corrects inherited tendencies, including recognition of human and animal equality.
The move shows how a naturalistic worldview can accommodate objective truth, widespread error, and moral progress without appealing to a divine source.
Craig's claim that only a transcendent moral standard avoids sociocultural relativism and grounds condemnation across cultures.
Kagan accepts that societies may have appalling codes and compares moral progress to scientific progress, with reflective reasoning overcoming evolutionarily inherited starting beliefs.

God's nature and commands ground objective values and duties, while naturalism cannot adequately explain intrinsic human worth, categorical prescriptions, free moral agency, or ultimate accountability.
This closing synthesis consolidates the principal affirmative case across every major component of the motion and directly contests the adequacy of secular foundations.
Kagan's secular account claiming objective morality, duties, significance, and practical reasons without theistic grounding.
Craig concludes that God's holy nature, divine commands, and eternal consequences furnish morality, whereas naturalism reduces value to convention and duties to etiquette-like rules.
Objective morality and genuine present value do not require theism or eternal cosmic significance, because finite loving relationships and actions can possess real value despite eventual extinction.
The conclusion directly answers the motion by separating objective moral significance from cosmic permanence and denying that theistic belief is essential to morality.
Craig's inference that without theism and eternal consequences human actions lack objective moral significance.
Kagan closes by reaffirming robust objective morality and arguing that future death and cosmic extinction do not erase the current genuine value of love and moral action.
